items.title: Jingle Bells (chorus)
items.findings: No words in the file (the chorus is innocent). Research published in 2017 traced its first known performance to a blackface minstrel show in Boston in 1857; others dispute the reading.
items.suggestion: Keep; give the teacher a short note on the disputed history.

items.title: When the Saints Go Marching In
items.findings: No words in the file. A Christian spiritual about the day of judgement.
items.suggestion: Keep; label it a spiritual, as above.

items.title: Lucy Locket
items.findings: Kitty Fisher, named in the rhyme, was an eighteenth-century London courtesan, and the rhyme is said to begin as a joke about her. The words themselves are innocent.
items.suggestion: Keep as written; no change needed. A note for the teacher at most.

items.title: Au Clair de la Lune
items.findings: No words in the file. The later French verses (Lubin and the brunette) are mildly suggestive.
items.suggestion: Keep; if words are added, use the first verse only.

items.title: Canoinha nova
items.subtitle: Brazilian children's circle song — provisional plate reading
items.findings: Verse 1 (the new canoe that fell into the sea) is plain. Verse 2: "Pra sinh'Aninha cheirar": sinhá was the form of address enslaved people used for the master's wife or daughter. Verses 2 and 3 are courting verses (a carnation at the window; "Menina dos olhos grandes / Não olhe pra mim chorando").
items.suggestion: Teach verse 1, which is plain, once the plate reading is checked; leave verses 2 and 3 for a Brazilian educator, with a note on sinhá's history. Do not invent replacement words here.
items.source: Mário de Andrade, Ensaio sobre música brasileira (São Paulo: I. Chiarato & Cia., 1928), p. 36 (scan p. 46)

sourceUrls.label: Wikimedia Commons scan of the Ensaio, at scan page 46

items.title: Carry banana
items.subtitle: Jamaican ring tune
items.findings: "a Chiney banana": Jekyll explains it is a variety, the China banana ("a stout low kind which withstands wind"), but "Chiney" can be heard as a mocking word for Chinese people.
items.suggestion: Sing "China banana", Jekyll's own word for it in his note, and record the change in the N: line and in review-decision.
items.source: Walter Jekyll (ed.), Jamaican Song and Story (London: David Nutt, 1907), Project Gutenberg #35410 (music as MusicXML), no. XCIII, p. 196

sourceUrls.label: Project Gutenberg #35410: Jamaican Song and Story, with page images and the music

items.title: Soldier's Joy
items.findings: No words in the file. American sung verses mention morphine and beer ("twenty-five cents for the morphine").
items.suggestion: Keep as an instrumental with the note. It is the shorter of the two Soldier's Joy entries; keep both, or keep this one for the first tunes and the full Nottingham reel for later.

items.title: Amazing Grace
items.findings: No words in the file. A Christian hymn; its author, John Newton, had been a slave-ship captain before he became a clergyman and abolitionist, which is often taught with it.
items.suggestion: Keep; label it a hymn, like Jubilate Deo, so teachers can follow their school's guidance on religious songs.

items.title: Oh! Susanna
items.findings: No words in the file. Stephen Foster wrote it in 1848 for blackface minstrel shows, and his original second verse uses a racial slur in a joke about an explosion that kills five hundred Black people. Anyone who looks up the words can find it.
items.suggestion: Keep it out of the course. If a teacher wants the tune, play the melody only and teach the minstrel history with it; never the original words.

items.title: Greensleeves
items.findings: No words in the file. The old ballad's Lady Greensleeves is sometimes read as a woman of loose reputation; the tune is also the carol What Child Is This.
items.suggestion: Keep; no change needed.

items.title: Rama's lullaby
items.subtitle: Maratha lullaby
items.findings: A Maratha lullaby to the infant Rama as Vishnu ("It was Vishnu's self that was born on the lap of Kaushalya"), with devas strewing flowers: Hindu devotional words.
items.suggestion: Keep; label it a devotional lullaby, as above.
items.source: Fox Strangways, The Music of Hindostan (1914), Ex. 161, p. 66

sourceUrls.label: archive.org scan of The Music of Hindostan, at p. 66

items.title: Cuckoo's Nest
items.findings: No words in the file. "The Cuckoo's Nest" is also the title of a bawdy folk song in which the phrase is sexual slang.
items.suggestion: Keep the hornpipe as an instrumental; add a note "play the tune; the sung words are not for class", and leave the title.

items.title: Konpira fune fune
items.subtitle: Japanese game song
items.findings: No words in the file. The zashiki-asobi it belongs to is traditionally a drinking game at geisha parties in Kotohira: the player who hesitates drinks.
items.suggestion: Keep the tune and the hand game; reword the dossier from "party game" to "a party hand game from Kotohira" and teach the touching game only.
items.source: Nagai Iwai and Obata Kenhachiro (eds.), 1895, via Daisyfield.com transcription (Tom Potter, 2008, donated to the public domain)

items.title: Lalishrita
items.subtitle: Tamil lullaby, from a phonogram
items.findings: A Tamil lullaby that lays the baby at the feet of Sriranga (Vishnu at Srirangam): Hindu devotional words (Fox Strangways's singing translation; stanza 2: "I lay thee there at Sriranga raja's feet, full sure of His tender care").
items.suggestion: Keep; label it a devotional lullaby so teachers can follow their school's guidance on religious songs.
items.source: Fox Strangways, The Music of Hindostan (1914), Ex. 155, p. 64

sourceUrls.label: archive.org scan of The Music of Hindostan, at p. 64

items.title: Little Sally Water
items.subtitle: Jamaican ring game
items.findings: Last verse: a mock wedding ("Now you married I give you joy, first a gal an' second a boy") ending "give her a kiss an' send her out". Mild, and common in playground versions.
items.suggestion: Keep the full text in the file as the source, and end the class version before "Now you married" (the ring game works without it).
items.source: Walter Jekyll (ed.), Jamaican Song and Story (London: David Nutt, 1907), Project Gutenberg #35410 (music as MusicXML), no. LXXXIX, p. 191

sourceUrls.label: Project Gutenberg #35410: Jamaican Song and Story, with page images and the music

items.title: Meu barco é veleiro
items.subtitle: Paraíba coco — provisional plate reading
items.findings: The second half is a courting line about complexion: "Eu amo a cor morena / A cor morena é que me ama" (I love the brown colour; the brown colour loves me). Morena is an everyday, affectionate word in Brazil, but like the "mulata" of Sambalele it ties a love song to skin colour.
items.suggestion: Keep it out of the published set until a Brazilian educator (and the coco reviewer the dossier names) says how classes sing it today; the tune itself is a good tonic-arpeggio study. Do not invent replacement words here.
items.source: Mário de Andrade, Ensaio sobre música brasileira (São Paulo: I. Chiarato & Cia., 1928), p. 75 (scan p. 85)

sourceUrls.label: Wikimedia Commons scan of the Ensaio, at scan page 85

items.title: Mīkhāhī labu?
items.subtitle: Do you want hot beetroot? (Persian folk song)
items.findings: Verse 1, line 2: "sarat havu biaram?" (shall I bring a second wife over your head?). Verse 2: "qeri-to doshak biaram?", Strettell: "A new mattress by thine to-night?" (bedroom innuendo). Verses 3 and 4: cigarettes ("sigar"). The refrain "na-na-i" is clean. The dossier wrongly says verses 2 to 4 are fine.
items.suggestion: Correct the dossier first. For class, sing only the first line ("mikhahi labu biaram?", shall I bring you hot beetroot?) with the refrain, or choose another of Fairchild's twelve songs after reading its words.
items.source: Blair Fairchild (coll. and arr.), Twelve Persian Folk-Songs (London: Novello, 1904), no. 4, pp. 15-17; English words by Alma Strettell; University of Rochester scan

sourceUrls.label: IMSLP: Twelve Persian Folk-Songs (Novello, 1904), Sibley Library (Rochester) scan

items.title: Nirguna's lullaby
items.subtitle: Maratha lullaby
items.findings: No words under the notes; the title names Nirguna, the supreme being in Hindu thought, and the book's prose translation is a tired mother's lullaby (celestial carpenters made the cradle; my baby is not yet asleep).
items.suggestion: Keep; label it a devotional lullaby. Nothing in the words to change.
items.source: Fox Strangways, The Music of Hindostan (1914), Ex. 162, pp. 66-67

sourceUrls.label: archive.org scan of The Music of Hindostan, at p. 66

items.title: Soldiers' Joy
items.findings: No words in the file. The same sung verses as the other Soldier's Joy (morphine and beer).
items.suggestion: Keep as an instrumental with the note. The arranger test uses this tune; it reads it from here while it is in review.

items.title: Sugar in the Gourd
items.findings: No words in the file. Sung versions of this old-time tune have a sexual double meaning.
items.suggestion: Keep as an instrumental with the same note: play the tune, not the words.

items.title: Sambalelê
items.subtitle: Brazilian roda
items.findings: Verse I: "Sambalele precisava e dumas boas lambadas" (Sambalele needed a good thrashing). The chorus sings "mulata" four times ("Pisa, pisa, pisa, mulata ... na barra da saia, mulata"), a word for a mixed-race woman with a colonial and racial history; verses II and III court a "mulata bonita" (how does one court? where do you live?).
items.suggestion: Keep it out of the published set until a Brazilian educator gives the words classes sing today. Choosing other verses is not enough, because "mulata" is in the chorus; do not invent replacement words here.
items.source: Mário de Andrade, Ensaio sobre a música brasileira (São Paulo: I. Chiarato, 1928), p. 38 (pdf p. 48), Wikimedia Commons scan

sourceUrls.label: Wikimedia Commons scan of the Ensaio, at scan page 48

items.title: The ayah's song
items.subtitle: Hindostani song from the steamer
items.findings: No words. Our N: line quotes Fox Strangways calling the singer, a domestic servant on a colonial steamer, "an unmusical ayah": colonial condescension, in our notes rather than in the song.
items.suggestion: Keep the melody; rephrase that note in our own words (one of the songs an ayah, a children's nurse, sang on board a steamer; the book says she lost her key and the songs were hard to piece together) and restore.
items.source: Fox Strangways, The Music of Hindostan (1914), Ex. 160, p. 66

sourceUrls.label: archive.org scan of The Music of Hindostan, at p. 66

items.title: Jubilate Deo (round)
items.findings: A round on the Latin psalm Jubilate Deo (Psalm 100, "Rejoice in God"); no words in the file.
items.suggestion: Keep; label it a sacred round so teachers can follow their school's guidance on religious songs.
